title: Differentiable Schwarz-Coupled Solvers for Thin Boundary Layer Transport: Inverse Modeling via Agentic AI Optimization
authors: Siva Viknesh, Amirhossein Arzani
abstract: High-Péclet-number transport problems give rise to thin boundary layers with steep near-wall gradients whose accurate solution requires high-resolution meshes and could challenge inverse modeling. To address this challenge, we develop an overlapping Schwarz domain-decomposition framework grounded in perturbation theory, in which an inner equation governs near-wall dynamics and an outer equation governs bulk transport, and both subproblems are discretized using the finite element method and assembled into a fully differentiable multidomain physics solver. The formulation permits coarser mesh resolutions, reducing computational cost relative to a single-domain formulation. Exploiting the differentiability of the coupled solver, we formulate inverse problems in which the governing equations and boundary conditions are imposed as hard constraints, with the Schwarz coupling enforcing interface continuity. To accelerate the resulting adjoint-based optimization, we integrate large language models (LLMs) into the inverse workflow in two distinct configurations: a standalone optimizer that proposes successive parameter updates from the adjoint-computed sensitivities and an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) approach with access to the complete solver workflow, enabling it to perform multistage optimization procedures. The agentic AI configuration is shown to be most advantageous when the spatially varying unknown is represented in a functional basis rather than a high-dimensional nodal field representation. In this case, the AI agent grows the library of candidate basis functions during optimization under a prescribed admission policy, admitting predefined families in stages and initializing their parameters. In short, our proposed framework integrates Schwarz-coupled differentiable physics with agentic AI optimization for the inverse modeling of multiscale transport problems.

infographic.key_insight: A differentiable overlapping Schwarz solver couples near-wall and bulk transport models, enabling inverse modeling of thin boundary layers with coarser meshes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could reduce computational costs when inferring spatially varying transport properties in high-Péclet-number engineering flows.
method: Discretize perturbation-based inner and outer transport equations with finite elements and couple them through overlapping Schwarz iterations.
Use adjoint sensitivities for inverse optimization, imposing governing equations and boundary conditions as hard constraints.
Integrate LLM-driven updates or a workflow-level AI agent that expands a functional basis under staged admission rules.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports lower computational cost than a single-domain formulation and greater agentic-AI benefit for functional-basis unknowns than nodal fields, but provides no quantitative benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on the unknown's representation and basis-admission policy; gains should not be assumed for high-dimensional nodal fields.
infographic.paper_title: Differentiable Schwarz-Coupled Solvers for Thin Boundary Layer Transport: Inverse Modeling via Agentic AI Optimization

title: Triadic energy cascades and linear amplification mechanisms in supersonic turbulent boundary layers over curved walls
authors: Lucas Feitosa de Souza, Hugo F. da Silva Lui, William Roberto Wolf, Pedro Stefanin Volpiani
abstract: Direct numerical simulations are performed to investigate supersonic turbulent boundary layers subjected to continuous concave and convex surface curvatures. Scale-resolved spectral turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) budgets, triadic energy-transfer bispectra, spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD), and global resolvent analysis are employed to elucidate the effects of compressibility and pressure gradients, and to distinguish the linear and nonlinear mechanisms at play. Over concave walls, the destabilizing curvature enhances pressure-strain redistribution, shifting near-wall turbulence toward a two-component state, and induces a shear-driven outer-layer production peak at low spanwise wavenumbers. Bispectral and SPOD analyses reveal that this outer-layer energy feeds a structured, multi-step triadic transfer toward fundamental large-scale and spanwise-uniform modes, which physically manifests as streamwise vortex breakdown rather than a three-dimensional inverse cascade. Global resolvent analysis further demonstrates that while nonlinear triadic interactions select the dominant scale amplitudes, the spatial topology of these coherent structures is dictated by linear mean-flow receptivity and spatially developing convective instabilities. Conversely, over convex walls, stabilizing curvature and dilatation attenuate pressure fluctuations and suppress pressure-strain redistribution, breaking the near-wall turbulent cycle and trapping energy within elongated, one-component streamwise streaks, while a localized resolvent wavemaker energizes the downstream recovery region.

infographic.key_insight: Wall curvature reshapes supersonic boundary-layer turbulence: concave walls promote structured triadic energy transfer and vortex breakdown, while convex walls suppress redistribution and retain energy in elongated streamwise streaks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Distinguishing nonlinear scale selection from linear flow receptivity can inform turbulence modeling and flow-control strategies for curved supersonic surfaces.
method: Direct numerical simulations over continuously concave and convex walls.
Scale-resolved TKE budgets, triadic-transfer bispectra, and spectral proper orthogonal decomposition.
Global resolvent analysis to identify linear amplification and coherent-structure topology.
infographic.evidence_signal: DNS-based diagnostics reveal a low-spanwise-wavenumber outer-layer production peak over concave walls and suppressed pressure-strain redistribution over convex walls.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no parameter ranges or quantitative validation metrics, limiting assessment of generalization to other Mach numbers, Reynolds numbers, and curvature profiles.
infographic.paper_title: Triadic energy cascades and linear amplification mechanisms in supersonic turbulent boundary layers over curved walls

title: Agentic AI Reasoning and Learned Sampling for Task-Aware Projection Selection in Sparse-View CT: Predicting Hemodynamics
authors: Mahmoud Elhadidy, Roshan M. D'Souza, Amirhossein Arzani
abstract: Sparse-view computed tomography (CT) reduces the number of acquired projections, but conventional sampling strategies are designed primarily for image reconstruction rather than for downstream physical inference. Here, we investigate optimal task-aware projection selection for directly predicting hemodynamics from sparse CT angiography (CTA) measurements. Using computational fluid dynamics simulations of intracranial aneurysms, we generate synthetic fan-beam CTA projections and train a Fourier neural operator (FNO) to predict two targets: the spatially resolved time-averaged wall shear stress (TAWSS) field and the spatially averaged TAWSS. The FNO was coupled with optimal input selection for simultaneous optimal sampling and training. Our goal was to investigate if agentic AI could discover optimal sampling strategies that outperform current methods. We compared fixed uniform and golden-angle sampling with three task-aware optimal selection strategies: Gumbel-Softmax, a Soft top-K method, and an agentic AI selector. The methods were compared at different view selection budgets. A detailed analysis of the AI agent was performed to understand its reasoning and performance. For spatially resolved TAWSS, Agentic and Soft top-K achieve the lowest mean errors (Agentic performs slightly better) and substantially outperform fixed sampling under extreme sparsity. For spatially averaged TAWSS, optimized selection becomes important at extremely sparse acquisitions. Analysis of the selected masks reveals multiple distinct subsets concentrated around informative regions. Moreover, masks optimized for hemodynamic prediction yield poor image reconstructions, showing that task-optimal acquisition differs fundamentally from reconstruction-optimal acquisition. This work suggests the possibility of designing sparse acquisitions directly around downstream physical quantities.

infographic.key_insight: Task-aware CT projection selection improves direct hemodynamic prediction under extreme sparsity, but its optimal views differ from those needed for image reconstruction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Sparse CTA acquisition could be tailored to predict aneurysm wall shear stress rather than to maximize reconstructed image quality.
method: Generate synthetic fan-beam CTA projections from intracranial aneurysm CFD simulations.
Train a Fourier neural operator to predict spatially resolved and spatially averaged time-averaged wall shear stress.
Compare uniform and golden-angle sampling with Gumbel-Softmax, Soft top-K, and agentic AI selection across view budgets.
infographic.evidence_signal: On synthetic CFD-derived data, agentic AI and Soft top-K achieved the lowest mean spatial-field errors, with agentic AI slightly better and both substantially outperforming fixed sampling under extreme sparsity.
infographic.watch_item: Clinical generalization remains unestablished by the synthetic-data evaluation, and hemodynamics-optimized views produced poor image reconstructions.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic AI Reasoning and Learned Sampling for Task-Aware Projection Selection in Sparse-View CT: Predicting Hemodynamics

title: Inherent Failure Modes of Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Buoyancy-Driven Flow: Role of Non-Dimensionalization in Network Training
authors: Krishan Chand, Ahmad Peyvan, Haoxiang Luo
abstract: We investigate the influence of non-dimensionalization on the trainability and accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for buoyancy-driven flows. Using a differentially heated square cavity at $\mathrm{Pr}=0.71$ and $\mathrm{Ra}=10^3$--$10^5$, we compare thermal-diffusive and free-fall velocity scalings under identical training conditions. The free-fall scaling, with a unit buoyancy coefficient, achieves errors below 1.1\% in the mean Nusselt number for $\mathrm{Ra}\le10^4$, whereas the diffusive scaling, with a buoyancy coefficient of $\mathrm{Ra}\,\mathrm{Pr}$, produces errors of 157--650\% and diverges at $\mathrm{Ra}=10^5$. We identify a coefficient-induced gradient imbalance, with the dominant buoyancy-related contribution to the loss gradient scaling as $(\mathrm{Ra}\,\mathrm{Pr})^2$, and confirm it through direct gradient measurements. Neither sparse-data supervision nor adaptive loss weighting resolves the training difficulties under the tested conditions. For unsteady convection, the free-fall PINN accurately predicts long-time heat transfer but fails to capture the transient Nusselt-number overshoot. These findings establish non-dimensionalization as an important design consideration for improving PINN trainability in buoyancy-driven flows.

infographic.key_insight: Non-dimensionalization can determine PINN trainability: free-fall scaling limits buoyancy-driven gradient imbalance that undermines thermal-diffusive scaling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Choosing physically appropriate scaling can improve PINN predictions of buoyancy-driven heat transfer without changing the training setup.
method: Compare thermal-diffusive and free-fall scalings under identical training conditions.
Evaluate differentially heated square-cavity flow at Pr = 0.71 and Ra = 10³–10⁵.
Measure loss gradients and test sparse-data supervision and adaptive loss weighting.
infographic.evidence_signal: For Ra ≤ 10⁴, free-fall scaling yields mean Nusselt-number errors below 1.1%, versus 157–650% for thermal-diffusive scaling, which diverges at Ra = 10⁵.
infographic.watch_item: Free-fall scaling still misses the transient Nusselt-number overshoot in unsteady convection despite accurate long-time heat transfer.
infographic.paper_title: Inherent Failure Modes of Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Buoyancy-Driven Flow: Role of Non-Dimensionalization in Network Training

title: Regional accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for recirculation in a deep lid-driven cavity
authors: Ehsan Roohi, Christopher J. McDevitt
abstract: Deep lid-driven cavities contain strong motion beneath the lid and much weaker recirculation at depth, so agreement in bulk velocity is an incomplete assessment of a computed flow. We examine data-free physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for steady, two-dimensional incompressible flow in a cavity of depth-to-width ratio five at Reynolds numbers 100, 250, 500 and 1000. An established hard-constrained streamfunction formulation is combined with prescribed regional collocation, transferred initialization, and selected residual-scaling and envelope variants. Independent spectral/$hp$ calculations with the same Gaussian-regularized lid provide the reference fields. For a cavity of depth-to-width ratio $D/W=5$ at Reynolds numbers $\mathrm{Re}=100$, 250, 500, and 1000, evaluation on a common $121\times605$ grid gives interior relative velocity discrepancies of 5.130\%--7.850\%. Over the same cases, floor-region relative velocity discrepancies remain below 5\%, with absolute RMS discrepancies ranging from $1.255\times10^{-10}U$ to $2.332\times10^{-9}U$, where $U$ is the lid-velocity scale. In a separate $161\times801$ assessment at $\Rey=1000$, the refined workflow lowers interior velocity discrepancy from 5.624\% to 2.658\% and gauge-aligned pressure RMS discrepancy from $2.793\times10^{-3}$ to $1.167\times10^{-3}ρU^2$. The improvements compare accumulated training workflows and do not isolate regional sampling. Configuration rankings depend on both region and observable. These finite-budget comparisons establish where the retained workflows agree with the reference and where rotational-field discrepancies remain substantial.

infographic.key_insight: Data-free PINNs capture velocity in a deep lid-driven cavity, but accuracy varies by region and observable, with substantial rotational-field discrepancies remaining.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Deep-cavity flow predictions need regional validation because bulk velocity agreement can obscure errors in weak recirculation far below the lid.
method: Hard-constrained streamfunction PINNs for steady 2D incompressible flow at depth-to-width ratio 5 and Re = 100–1000.
Prescribed regional collocation, transferred initialization, and selected residual-scaling and envelope variants.
Validation against independent spectral/hp reference fields using the same Gaussian-regularized lid.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a 121×605 grid, interior relative velocity discrepancies were 5.130–7.850% and floor-region discrepancies stayed below 5%; a separate 161×801 evaluation at Re = 1000 showed refinement reducing interior discrepancy from 5.624% to 2.658%.
infographic.watch_item: Improvements compare accumulated training workflows rather than isolating regional sampling, and configuration rankings depend on region and observable.
infographic.paper_title: Regional accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for recirculation in a deep lid-driven cavity

title: An Optimal Seed Reveals the Dynamical Route to Spontaneous Splitting of Turbulent Puffs
authors: Chihang Liu, Hao Ni, Jiashun Guan
abstract: The localized turbulence in pipe flow, known as puffs, is sustained by their proliferation. This process is crucial to the subcritical laminar-turbulent transition, a century-old fundamental problem related to a wide range of natural and engineered systems. Here, we leverage the nonlinear nonmodal analysis of a reduced-order model to capture the full Navier-Stokes dynamics of the splitting process: from the splitting seed through the edge state to successful splitting, even when the pre-edge evolution is obscured by the puff's intrinsic chaotic fluctuations. Moreover, the optimized evolution provides a splitting-progress coordinate to frame a phase-space representation of the proliferation, resolving the temporal desynchronization among chaotic realizations and thereby enabling dynamically aligned ensemble averaging to uncover the underlying splitting dynamics. The splitting seed is characterized by a strong velocity inflection, and its energy threshold exhibits a power-law scaling with the Reynolds number, giving the optimal solution direct physical consistency in spontaneous puff splitting.

infographic.key_insight: An optimized perturbation reveals how a turbulent pipe-flow puff evolves through an edge state into a successful split, despite chaotic fluctuations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Understanding puff proliferation can inform prediction of the laminar–turbulent transition in pipe flows relevant to fluid transport systems.
method: Apply nonlinear nonmodal analysis to a reduced-order model to identify an optimal splitting seed.
Trace the splitting route from seed through edge state to successful proliferation.
Use a splitting-progress coordinate to dynamically align chaotic realizations for ensemble averaging.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports recovery of the full Navier–Stokes splitting dynamics, a strong velocity inflection in the seed, and power-law scaling of its energy threshold with Reynolds number.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify the tested Reynolds-number range or quantitative validation errors, limiting assessment of generalizability.
infographic.paper_title: An Optimal Seed Reveals the Dynamical Route to Spontaneous Splitting of Turbulent Puffs

title: Predicting Sparse Observables in Parameterized Unsteady Flows Using Coarse-Mesh Graph Neural Networks
authors: Brener Ramos, William R. Wolf, Tarcísio C. D. Oliveira, Scott T. M. Dawson
abstract: Full-order surrogates for high-dimensional nonlinear flows are often unnecessary when applications require only selected degrees of freedom. We propose reduced-order models that bypass full-state reconstruction by deploying graph neural networks (GNNs) directly on coarse meshes. Applied to parameterized 2D/3D confined cylinder flows and an unevenly heated cavity over Reynolds/Rayleigh-number ranges, the models generalize to unseen conditions and accurately predict sparse probe locations and integrated quantities. Coarse-mesh GNNs match or outperform finer-mesh surrogates while reducing training time and memory, even for 3D chaotic dynamics. A dynamics-informed adaptive sampling strategy guided by frequency-spectrum variations reduces maximum errors by an order of magnitude versus uniform sampling at negligible cost. Coarse-mesh training also makes noise-augmented multi-step unrolling practical, improving long-horizon autoregressive predictions. The approach outperforms parametric DMD, sparse MLPs, U-Nets, and Fourier neural operators at lower cost, and enables system identification and state estimation from sparse observations. These results show that coarse-mesh representations, adaptive sampling, and noise-augmented unrolled training form an efficient framework for reduced-order modeling of parameterized unsteady flows without solver-resolution reconstruction.

infographic.key_insight: Coarse-mesh graph neural networks predict sparse flow observables without reconstructing the full flow field, matching or outperforming finer-mesh surrogates at lower training cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports efficient prediction, system identification, and state estimation when engineers need only selected probes or integrated flow quantities.
method: Train graph neural networks directly on coarse meshes to predict sparse observables.
Select training parameters adaptively using variations in flow frequency spectra.
Use noise-augmented multi-step unrolling to improve long-horizon autoregressive predictions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on parameterized 2D/3D confined cylinder flows and an unevenly heated cavity showed generalization to unseen conditions; adaptive sampling reduced maximum errors by an order of magnitude versus uniform sampling.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization beyond the tested geometries and Reynolds/Rayleigh-number ranges remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Predicting Sparse Observables in Parameterized Unsteady Flows Using Coarse-Mesh Graph Neural Networks

title: Optimization of curved vortex generator geometry for enhanced thermal performance in water-to-air finned-tube heat exchanger
authors: Josip Batista, Anica Trp, Kristian Lenić, Mateo Kirinčić
abstract: In the study, the geometry of curved rectangular vortex generators (RVG) has been optimized to enhance heat transfer and overall performance of the analyzed water-to-air finned-tube heat exchanger (FTHE). The developed and validated conjugate numerical model includes a small section of the full-scale heat exchanger representing the computational domain, with fully developed velocity and temperature profiles specified at the inlet boundaries of the water. Four influential geometry parameters of the vortex generator were selected for the optimization; attack angle, curvature angle, axial position in the streamwise direction and height. The optimization process has been performed according to two criteria: maximization of heat transfer solely and maximization of heat transfer while considering the influence of pressure drop. Accordingly, one objective function related to the Colburn factor (j) and two objective functions combining the Colburn factor and the friction factor (f) were defined. The regression analysis has been used and the Central composite design of experiment was selected in order to obtain non-linear regression polynomial functions which were integrated into the investigated objectives. The optimization procedure has been performed using the genetic algorithm. Optimized configurations performance improvement was evaluated through comparison with the performance of the reference FTHE with plain fins. For the RVG configuration optimized according to the objective of maximizing heat transfer, the Colburn factor was enhanced by 53.1%. Optimizing the RVG configuration to maximize heat transfer while accounting for the influence of pressure drop resulted in an enhancement of the FTHE area goodness factor by 14.4% for one set of geometry parameters, and an enhancement of volume goodness factor by 26.5% for another.

infographic.key_insight: Optimizing curved rectangular vortex generators increased the Colburn heat-transfer factor by 53.1%, while separate pressure-drop-aware optimizations improved area and volume goodness factors by 14.4% and 26.5%, respectively.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Tailored vortex-generator geometry can improve water-to-air finned-tube heat exchanger performance while balancing heat-transfer gains against pressure-drop penalties.
method: Used a validated conjugate numerical model of a representative heat exchanger section.
Applied central composite experimental design and nonlinear polynomial regression to four geometry variables: attack angle, curvature angle, axial position and height.
Used a genetic algorithm to optimize heat-transfer-only and pressure-drop-aware objectives.
infographic.evidence_signal: Performance gains were evaluated numerically against a reference heat exchanger with plain fins, with different optimized geometries yielding the reported improvements.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish whether the optimized geometries retain their benefits across operating conditions or in full-scale experimental tests.
infographic.paper_title: Optimization of curved vortex generator geometry for enhanced thermal performance in water-to-air finned-tube heat exchanger

title: Free-vortex-wake dynamics of airborne wind energy kites in crosswind flight
authors: Yinong Tian, Shan Wang
abstract: The wake of an airborne wind energy kite is shaped by its crosswind path and, for on-board generation, by the slipstreams of its rotors, and in farms it reaches downstream units. It is computed here by a vortex step method with a time-marching free vortex wake, implemented by the authors in their open-source code OpenFAWE with a lumped-mass tether, actuator-disc rotors releasing vortex rings and several kites. It reproduces an independent vortex step code to 10^-9 on the rigid-wing Makani M600 and within 0.3% in lift and 0.9% in drag on the TU Delft V3 leading-edge inflatable kite, matching its Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes lift within 3.1%. For fixed kites the lift deficit of a finite wake is the far field of its starting vortex, which fixes the wake length before a run, and the vortex core must stay below the narrowest panel width. With these settings the helical tip-vortex pair of the M600 on its loop lowers its lift by about 0.5% from 5 to 13 m/s. Free rotor rings do not converge with the time step, whereas an undeformed slipstream tube converges once its rings are refined at the wing and raises the lift by 1.9%. A slipstream deflected by the wing lowers it by 3.5%, so the treatment near the wing sets the sign of the rotor effect. A second unit one loop diameter downstream loses 0.5% of its lift and 2.2% of its aerodynamic power, with or without rotors.

infographic.key_insight: Crosswind kite wakes modestly reduce lift, but rotor-slipstream treatment near the wing can reverse the predicted rotor effect.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reliable airborne wind energy load and farm-power predictions require careful wake sizing, vortex-core selection, and rotor–wing interaction modeling.
method: Vortex step aerodynamics coupled to a time-marching free vortex wake in OpenFAWE.
Lumped-mass tether and actuator-disc rotors represented by shed vortex rings.
Single- and multi-kite simulations assessing wake resolution and rotor-slipstream treatments.
infographic.evidence_signal: Validation showed lift agreement within 3.1% of RANS for the TU Delft V3 kite; a second unit one loop diameter downstream lost 0.5% lift and 2.2% aerodynamic power.
infographic.watch_item: Free rotor-ring simulations did not converge with time-step refinement, and alternative slipstream treatments shifted the predicted lift effect from +1.9% to −3.5%.
infographic.paper_title: Free-vortex-wake dynamics of airborne wind energy kites in crosswind flight

title: Aerodynamic Shape Optimization of unsteady flapping wings
authors: Hamid R. Karbasian, Brian C. Vermeire
abstract: This study introduces a new approach for building surrogate models, in the form of Reduced Order Models (ROMs), for PDE-constrained optimization. A physics-constrained data-driven framework is developed to transform large-scale non-linear optimization problems into ROM-constrained optimization problems. Unlike conventional methods, which suffer from instability of the forward sensitivity function, the proposed approach projects optimization problems to system dynamics optimization problems in Hilbert space to increase stability, diminish memory requirements, and lower computational cost. The present approach is applied to shape optimization of a 2D flapping wing section at $Re=2,400$, where the non-linear interaction of the wing with fluid includes chaotic flow structures. It is shown that the proposed approach can significantly enhance the time-averaged thrust force and propulsive efficiency by 37\% and 40\%, respectively. We also tested this approach for a 3D flapping wing and the results reveal the potential of the proposed approach for more complex optimal designs in the aerospace industry.

infographic.key_insight: A physics-constrained, data-driven reduced-order modeling framework enables aerodynamic shape optimization of unsteady flapping wings while targeting greater stability and lower computational cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could make optimization of thrust and propulsive efficiency more practical for complex flapping-wing designs.
method: Replace large-scale PDE-constrained optimization with reduced-order-model-constrained optimization.
Project optimization into system dynamics optimization in Hilbert space to improve sensitivity stability.
Apply the framework to 2D wing-section shape optimization and test it on a 3D flapping wing.
infographic.evidence_signal: For a 2D flapping wing section at Re = 2,400 with chaotic flow structures, the abstract reports gains of 37% in time-averaged thrust and 40% in propulsive efficiency, plus a 3D test.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify computational savings or 3D performance gains, leaving scalability and broader applicability to be assessed.
infographic.paper_title: Aerodynamic Shape Optimization of unsteady flapping wings

title: Causality-informed dynamic mode decomposition for unsteady flow analysis
authors: Yihua Pan, Jiaqing Kou
abstract: Causal analysis characterizes directional dependencies in dynamical systems, while such information is not typically used to inform reduced-order modeling of unsteady flows. This study proposes a Granger Causality-informed Dynamic Mode Decomposition (GC-DMD) framework that incorporates such information into data-driven modeling and modal analysis of high-dimensional flow data. The framework uses conditional Granger causality estimates to regularize the identification of the DMD operator, preferentially suppressing weakly supported interactions while preserving dynamically relevant couplings. This regularization promotes sparse operators informed by directional predictive dependencies, leading to improved predictive accuracy and identification of dynamically relevant modes. GC-DMD is evaluated on a linear system with a known coupling structure, lid-driven cavity flows with varying dynamical complexity, and a broadband transonic turbulent jet. Compared with standard DMD, GC-DMD improves operator identification accuracy in the linear benchmark and improves the robustness of the identified spectrum while reducing long-horizon prediction errors in the cavity flows. For the turbulent jet, it yields a sparser operator with improved prediction accuracy. These results demonstrate the potential of incorporating causality information to guide the identification of sparse, predictive reduced-order models of complex flows. The \href{https://github.com/JiaqingKou/GC-DMD-Granger-Causality-informed-DMD}{source codes} \footnote{https://github.com/JiaqingKou/GC-DMD-Granger-Causality-informed-DMD} from this research are publicly available in the GitHub repository.

infographic.key_insight: Granger causality-informed DMD uses directional predictive dependencies to identify sparse flow models with improved prediction accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could improve reduced-order prediction of complex unsteady flows while suppressing weakly supported interactions.
method: Estimate conditional Granger causality from flow data.
Use causality estimates to regularize DMD operator identification.
Extract dynamically relevant modes from the resulting sparse operator.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on a known linear system, lid-driven cavity flows, and a broadband transonic turbulent jet showed improvements over standard DMD in operator identification, spectral robustness, or prediction accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: Granger causality captures predictive dependence rather than physical causation, so inferred couplings require careful interpretation.
infographic.paper_title: Causality-informed dynamic mode decomposition for unsteady flow analysis

title: Nonlinear dynamics of short-wave instabilities in a helical vortex within and beyond the weakly nonlinear regime
authors: Daisuke Nishiyama, Yuji Hattori
abstract: The nonlinear evolution of a helical vortex with axial flow disturbed by an elliptic or curvature instability mode is investigated by direct numerical simulations. The normalized vortex core radius and reduced pitch are systematically varied to examine a wide range of linear growth rates, revealing two types of nonlinear evolution. At relatively small growth rates, both instabilities exhibit weakly nonlinear saturation, with the vortex and unstable mode structures largely preserved. Together with previous findings for other vortex configurations, these results reveal that weakly nonlinear saturation is a generic feature of short-wave instabilities. At larger growth rates, the instabilities reach higher energy levels and evolve beyond the weakly nonlinear regime, with the vortex and unstable mode structures substantially deformed. Comparison with weakly nonlinear analysis suggests that larger linear growth rates require larger disturbance amplitudes for nonlinear effects to balance linear growth. At these larger amplitudes, higher-order nonlinear effects and modal components not retained in the weakly nonlinear analysis become increasingly important, as demonstrated by the numerical results. This provides a new physical interpretation of the departure from the weakly nonlinear regime. Since helical vortices serve as a model for tip vortices shed from rotating blades, these results offer useful insights for tip-vortex control in wind turbines, which can potentially accelerate wake recovery and thereby improve turbine performance.

infographic.key_insight: Short-wave instabilities in helical vortices saturate weakly at lower linear growth rates but substantially deform the vortex at higher growth rates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These dynamics may inform wind-turbine tip-vortex control strategies aimed at accelerating wake recovery and improving performance.
method: Direct numerical simulations of helical vortices with axial flow.
Vary normalized core radius and reduced pitch for elliptic and curvature instability modes.
Compare nonlinear evolution with weakly nonlinear analysis.
infographic.evidence_signal: The parameter sweep reveals structure-preserving saturation at lower growth rates and stronger deformation, higher-order nonlinear effects, and additional modal contributions at higher rates.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports idealized vortex simulations, not an AI surrogate or validation of control strategies in turbine wakes.
infographic.paper_title: Nonlinear dynamics of short-wave instabilities in a helical vortex within and beyond the weakly nonlinear regime

title: Transition to turbulence in swirl created by a vertical magnetic field in liquid metal electrodes
authors: Uma Siva Sankar Kompalli, Avishek Ranjan, Suneet Singh
abstract: Flow transitions in electromagnetically-driven swirl in a cylindrical domain are investigated using three-dimensional simulations for a liquid metal battery electrode. The parameter space considered: applied current $I=11.11-100A$; Current density, $J_0 \approx 4,000-35,000 A/m^2$, domain radius, $R=3-9cm$, domain height, $H=3$ and $4.5cm$). The background magnetic field, $B_0$, strength is varied systematically from 0.1 to 20 G to characterize the route to chaos. \cite{davidson2022swirling} found the onset of chaos occurs around $1-1.5 G$ for aspect ratio $1/6$ and current of 100A, however, this is shifted to $16-17 G$ for a lower current of 16A and aspect ratio $1/2$. Across a range of geometrical configurations and forcing conditions, including variations in aspect ratio, current and current density, a consistent sequence of dynamical transitions is evident from phase portraits, FFT spectrum, 0-1 chaos test, autocorrelation function and correlation dimension. The flow evolution is by the Ruelle--Takens-Newhouse route to chaos, with the strange non-chaotic attractor (SNA) regime providing an intermediate state prior to the onset of chaos. In our results, it is observed that, for a fixed aspect ratio, the transition is governed by a dimensionless group, $Q_m$, representing the ratio of applied Lorentz force to viscous force. The critical value of $Q_m$ at the onset of oscillatory flow is found to be nearly invariant except when the domain height is varied. Moreover, our results follow the $Re \sim Q_m^{2/3}$ scaling law expected from torque balance moderately-forced electro-magnetically driven swirl flows.

infographic.key_insight: Magnetically driven swirl in liquid metal electrodes follows a Ruelle–Takens–Newhouse route to chaos, with an intermediate strange non-chaotic attractor regime.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The Lorentz-to-viscous force ratio Q_m helps organize flow transitions at fixed aspect ratio, informing electromagnetic flow control in liquid metal batteries.
method: Three-dimensional simulations of cylindrical liquid metal electrodes under applied currents of 11.11–100 A.
Varied vertical magnetic field from 0.1–20 G, cylinder radius from 3–9 cm, and height between 3 and 4.5 cm.
Diagnosed transitions using phase portraits, FFT spectra, the 0–1 chaos test, autocorrelation, and correlation dimension.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across simulated geometries and forcing conditions, the oscillation-onset Q_m was nearly invariant at fixed aspect ratio except when height changed, while Reynolds number followed Re ∼ Q_m^(2/3).
infographic.watch_item: Height-dependent onset thresholds limit a universal Q_m criterion, and experimental validation is not reported in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Transition to turbulence in swirl created by a vertical magnetic field in liquid metal electrodes

title: Identifiability Limits of Reynolds-Stress Attribution in Localized Nonorthogonal Flow Representations
authors: Peng Cheng, Ming Jian, Wen Tong
abstract: Reynolds stress is assembled from correlations among velocity fluctuations; assigning it to named vortical structures additionally requires their velocity fields to be separable. We examine this requirement in homogeneous isotropic turbulence from the Johns Hopkins Turbulence Databases (JHTDB) using a frozen solenoidal expansion of curl-lifted anisotropic Gaussian vorticity functions. The expansion retains locally addressable blob-, sheet-, and tube-like geometry, while its fixed Biot-Savart map carries coefficient covariance exactly into the stress of the represented Gaussian velocity. Principal-angle geometry and self-cross covariance then connect overlap between group velocity spans to stress assembly. At a principal cosine of 0.95, 55% of the sheet-associated directions are also closely represented by the tube-like family, and products within the shared directions carry 99.6% of the covariance cancellation. Removing between-family covariance increases the direct numerical simulation (DNS)-referenced stress error by factors of 53.6 to 87. Orthogonal Fourier and proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) regroupings of the same velocity remove this cancellation, showing that it follows from the local nonorthogonal organization rather than from the represented field alone. The morphology labels remain representation-dependent, but their physical consequence is direct: Reynolds stress in this local description is carried by coupled velocity fluctuations, not by additive component energies. Localized nonorthogonal representations can therefore reveal how turbulent momentum flux is assembled, provided that span overlap and cross covariance are retained.

infographic.key_insight: In a localized nonorthogonal flow representation, Reynolds stress comes from coupled velocity fluctuations, so separate structure energies cannot capture its assembly.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Structure-based turbulence analysis must retain overlap and cross covariance to avoid misleading momentum-flux attribution.
method: Represent JHTDB homogeneous isotropic turbulence using a frozen solenoidal expansion of curl-lifted anisotropic Gaussian vorticity functions.
Measure blob-, sheet-, and tube-like velocity-span overlap using principal angles and self-cross covariance.
Compare stress assembly with orthogonal Fourier and POD regroupings of the same velocity.
infographic.evidence_signal: At a principal cosine of 0.95, 55% of sheet-associated directions overlap closely with tube-like directions; shared-direction products carry 99.6% of covariance cancellation, and removing between-family covariance raises DNS-referenced stress error by factors of 53.6–87.
infographic.watch_item: Morphology labels and stress attribution are representation-dependent; these results do not establish unique physical contributions from named structures.
infographic.paper_title: Identifiability Limits of Reynolds-Stress Attribution in Localized Nonorthogonal Flow Representations

title: Kinetic linear stability theory for incompressible parallel shear flows with the full Boltzmann collision operator
authors: Vassilis Theofilis
abstract: Modal and non-modal linear stability analysis of incompressible shear flows is performed for the first time by linearizing the Boltzmann equation and its full collision operator. In this kinetic linear stability theory (kLST) the hard-sphere operator and its BGK, ES-BGK and Shakhov relaxation models share the same discretization, so that their results can be compared directly. Written in the peculiar velocity about a Chapman-Enskog base state, the collision operators are independent of the cross-stream coordinate and are formed once. Summation-by-parts Legendre collocation, weak diffuse-reflection wall conditions and a moment-consistent velocity derivative yield an energy-stable discrete operator, verified to spectral accuracy by a manufactured solution. Numerical solution of the four-dimensional problem, comparable in size to a TriGlobal problem (Theofilis 2011), is made feasible by the fast spectral method of Gamba, Haack, Hauck and Hu (2017) for the full operator. Modal kLST uses matrix-free shift-invert Arnoldi iteration, preconditioned by an exact relaxation-model inverse. Non-modal kLST is based on an energy norm containing Chu's disturbance energy, a kinetic Reynolds-Orr equation identifying the mean shear as the only energy source. Transient growth and pseudospectra follow from the same preconditioned solves. For plane Couette and Poiseuille flows, the mixing layer and the Blasius boundary layer at Reynolds numbers 10^2-10^5, all four operators recover the Orr-Sommerfeld eigenvalues (Orszag 1971; Mack 1976) in the incompressible limit to a few parts in 10^7 for the models and 10^6 for the full operator. The optimal growth of Butler and Farrell (1992) and the resolvent norms of Trefethen et al. (1993) are reproduced to 0.1%, while the pseudospectra converge where ill-conditioned eigenvalues do not.

infographic.key_insight: Linearizing the Boltzmann equation with its full collision operator recovers classical incompressible shear-flow stability and transient-growth results within a unified kinetic framework.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework enables direct comparison of full and simplified collision models for predicting disturbance amplification and instability in canonical shear flows.
method: Discretize full hard-sphere, BGK, ES-BGK and Shakhov operators using a shared, energy-stable formulation.
Combine fast spectral collision evaluation with matrix-free shift-invert Arnoldi and relaxation-model preconditioning.
Compute transient growth, resolvent norms and pseudospectra using a kinetic disturbance-energy norm.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four canonical flows at Reynolds numbers 10²–10⁵, incompressible-limit eigenvalues agree with benchmarks to a few parts in 10⁷ for relaxation models and 10⁶ for the full operator; optimal growth and resolvent norms agree within 0.1%.
infographic.watch_item: The four-dimensional kinetic problem remains computationally demanding, and validation reported here concerns canonical flows in the incompressible limit.
infographic.paper_title: Kinetic linear stability theory for incompressible parallel shear flows with the full Boltzmann collision operator

title: Effects of Deep Learning Architecture and Pretraining on Automated Vocal Fold Segmentation in Ex Vivo High-Speed Phonation Images
authors: Varun Vinayak Kalaiarasan, Charles Farbos de Luzan, Khalid Malik, Ephraim Gutmark, Liran Oren
abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) intraglottal particle image velocimetry (PIV) of ex vivo phonation experiments quantifies vocal fold medial surface dynamics and the intraglottal flow field. However, it relies on manual segmentation because residual glare, low tissue-to-flow contrast, and tracer-particle speckle obscure the vocal fold boundaries. This study assessed how deep learning architecture and ImageNet pretraining affect automated vocal fold segmentation in these high-speed images. Four established architectures from three categories were benchmarked: the convolutional neural network (CNN)-based UNet and UNet++, the hybrid CNN-transformer-based TransUNet, and the pure transformer-based Swin-UNet, the latter two trained from scratch and from ImageNet-pretrained weights. Using 16,344 expert-annotated images from 227 phonation trials of excised canine larynges, the six pipelines were trained with five seeds under a standardized protocol and compared on 50 held-out test trials using trial-level Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction. Mean Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) spanned only 0.9734 to 0.9764, so the pipelines differed mainly in boundary fidelity. Pretraining significantly improved the boundary F1 score (BF1) and 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) of the TransUNet and Swin-UNet, about four times more for the Swin-UNet. Once pretrained, the two performed similarly, although the Swin-UNet has only about a quarter of the trainable parameters. Without pretraining, the TransUNet had a significantly higher BF1 and a lower HD95 than both CNN-based pipelines and about half their share of images with HD95 > 50 pixels. To our knowledge, this is the first study to apply deep learning to vocal fold segmentation in 2D intraglottal PIV, and it offers a reference framework for segmenting experimental flow-visualization images with noisy optical conditions or highly deformable objects.

infographic.key_insight: ImageNet pretraining improved vocal fold boundary segmentation, bringing Swin-UNet to performance similar to pretrained TransUNet with roughly one-quarter of its trainable parameters.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Automated vocal fold segmentation could reduce manual processing in intraglottal PIV and support measurements of tissue dynamics and airflow under challenging optical conditions.
method: Benchmarked UNet, UNet++, TransUNet, and Swin-UNet across six pipelines.
Compared transformer-based models trained from scratch versus ImageNet-pretrained weights.
Evaluated overlap and boundary fidelity using DSC, BF1, and HD95.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using 16,344 expert-annotated images from 227 ex vivo canine phonation trials, pipelines were trained with five seeds and compared on 50 held-out trials using Holm-corrected, trial-level Wilcoxon tests; mean DSC ranged from 0.9734 to 0.9764.
infographic.watch_item: Validation was limited to ex vivo canine images; generalization to other imaging setups or in vivo conditions remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Effects of Deep Learning Architecture and Pretraining on Automated Vocal Fold Segmentation in Ex Vivo High-Speed Phonation Images

title: Generative AI in Turbulence: Foundations, Applications, Validations and Benchmarks
authors: Luca Biferale, Michele Buzzicotti
abstract: Generative AI offers new approaches to turbulence problems in which incomplete observations or unresolved d.o.f. admit multiple physically plausible solutions. Potential applications include stochastic closures, super-resolution, data assimilation, uncertainty quantification, and the generation of Eulerian and Lagrangian flow ensembles. However, turbulence is not a conventional image-generation problem. Its multiscale dynamics, intermittency, extreme events, rough velocity fields and intrinsically stochastic transport make visual realism, pointwise error, and low-order spectral agreement insufficient measures of physical fidelity. We examine where generative AI provide novel capabilities with emphasis on diffusion models, score-based methods, and related probability-transport formulations. We discuss their use in unconditional generation, probabilistic reconstruction, reduced-order modeling, temporal evolution, and mesh-free representations. We argue that validation must address turbulence properties: energy transfer, structure functions, anomalous scaling, pdf tails, coherent structures, conservation laws, temporal consistency, ensemble diversity and generalization. Finally, we discuss potential limitations in validation, baseline, data availability and reproducibility, and the need for a benchmark ecosystem combining open data, standardized challenges, hidden tests, physics-aware metrics, and documented failures. This paper serves as a bridge between two communities. For AI practitioners, we provide a fair and accessible introduction to turbulence, essential for appreciating the challenges posed by the field and for assessing the physical relevance of generative models. For turbulent practitioners, we provide an introduction to the key technological aspects of Generative AI, clarifying what these tools actually do, and where their potential and current limitations lie.

infographic.key_insight: Generative AI can represent multiple plausible turbulent flows, but physical fidelity requires validation beyond visual realism, pointwise error, and low-order spectra.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Potential uses include stochastic closures, super-resolution, data assimilation, and uncertainty quantification for incompletely observed or unresolved flows.
method: Review diffusion, score-based, and related probability-transport models.
Examine flow generation, probabilistic reconstruction, reduced-order modeling, and temporal evolution.
Outline turbulence-aware validation and shared benchmark requirements.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports no quantitative performance results; it advocates evaluation of energy transfer, intermittency, conservation, temporal consistency, ensemble diversity, and generalization.
infographic.watch_item: Limited data, weak baselines, and incomplete physical validation can obscure failures and undermine reproducibility.
infographic.paper_title: Generative AI in Turbulence: Foundations, Applications, Validations and Benchmarks

title: Wave Turbulence of Capillary Waves in Finite Systems
authors: Alexander O. Korotkevich
abstract: We consider classical problem of turbulence of capillary waves. In a series of numerical simulations it is shown that Zakharov-Filonenko spectrum corresponding to direct cascade of energy has a limited dynamic range of realization in a finite system, which shrinks with decreasing level of nonlinearity. Recent hypothesis that this dynamic range scales with average steepness as $\simμ^{8/3}$ is confirmed. As a byproduct the Zakharov-Filonenko spectrum was observed for record dynamic range close to or beyond one decade in a variety of simulation configurations.

infographic.key_insight: In finite systems, the Zakharov–Filonenko capillary-wave energy-cascade spectrum spans a limited dynamic range that shrinks with decreasing average steepness, consistent with ∼μ^(8/3) scaling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Finite-domain capillary-wave simulations must account for wave steepness when interpreting how broadly an energy-cascade spectrum can develop.
method: Numerically simulate capillary-wave turbulence in finite systems.
Evaluate the cascade spectrum across nonlinearity levels.
Test dynamic-range scaling with average wave steepness.
infographic.evidence_signal: The simulations confirm the proposed ∼μ^(8/3) scaling and show the Zakharov–Filonenko spectrum over a reported record dynamic range close to or beyond one decade across multiple configurations.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides numerical evidence but does not specify resolution, uncertainty estimates, or experimental validation.
infographic.paper_title: Wave Turbulence of Capillary Waves in Finite Systems

title: Toward fully stabilized flow control using deep reinforcement learning
authors: Wang Jia, Hang Xu
abstract: This study enhances the performance of flow control across various synthetic jet configurations by improving deep reinforcement learning techniques. The training results based on the foundational deep reinforcement learning framework indicate that as the Reynolds number increases, the effectiveness of synthetic jet control becomes increasingly sensitive to the position of the jet. When synthetic jets are positioned near the flow separation region, the control strategy consistently exhibits excellent performance. However, when synthetic jets are located farther from the separation region, the flow control performance diminishes, and the consumption of external energy increases. By enhancing dynamic state features and reshaping the reward function, we significantly improve control performance across various Reynolds numbers and synthetic jet positions. With the optimized framework, we achieve significant drag reduction effects ranging from 8% to 34% within the Reynolds number range of 100 to 400. The flow control strategy is capable of simultaneously achieving multiple control objectives, including reducing drag, suppressing lift, eliminating vortex shedding, and decreasing energy consumption. These findings highlight the potential of optimizing deep reinforcement learning frameworks to achieve more adaptive flow control strategies for various flow scenarios.

infographic.key_insight: Enhanced state features and reward shaping improve deep reinforcement learning flow control across synthetic jet positions, achieving 8%–34% drag reduction at Reynolds numbers of 100–400.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More adaptive synthetic jet control could reduce drag, lift fluctuations, vortex shedding, and actuation energy across varying flow conditions.
method: Train deep reinforcement learning controllers for multiple synthetic jet positions and Reynolds numbers.
Enhance dynamic state features to improve flow-state representation.
Reshape rewards to balance aerodynamic performance and energy consumption.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 8%–34% drag reduction over Reynolds numbers of 100–400 and improved control across tested jet positions.
infographic.watch_item: Performance beyond the tested Reynolds-number range and transfer to physical systems remain unestablished in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Toward fully stabilized flow control using deep reinforcement learning

title: From Stochastic Transport Models to High-Dimensional Bayesian Inference
authors: Dan Crisan, Oana Lang
abstract: The Stochastic Transport in Upper Ocean Dynamics project introduced a new paradigm for representing uncertainty in geophysical fluid dynamics through stochastic transport models calibrated from data. This paper provides a synthesis of the principal theoretical and data assimilation developments achieved as part of the project. The central theme of the paper is the transformation of stochastic transport models from a modelling paradigm into a mathematically rigorous framework equipped with analytical, variational, calibration and Bayesian data assimilation methodologies suitable for geophysical fluid dynamics. We describe the development of the theory of stochastic transport equations, including well-posedness, regularity and approximation results, together with their geometric foundations based on stochastic variational principles, rough paths and fractional transport models. We further review methodologies for calibrating stochastic transport structures from observational and high-resolution simulation data, ranging from reduced-order stochastic models to modern generative approaches. Finally, we discuss Bayesian inference and high-dimensional data assimilation techniques developed for stochastic transport models, including particle filter methodologies and machine learning uncertainty quantification. Taken together, these developments establish a coherent framework linking stochastic transport modelling, rigorous analysis, calibration and Bayesian inference, thereby providing a foundation for uncertainty quantification and forecasting in geophysical fluid dynamics.

infographic.key_insight: Stochastic transport models connect physically grounded uncertainty representation with rigorous analysis, data-driven calibration and high-dimensional Bayesian inference for geophysical flows.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This framework supports uncertainty quantification and forecasting in ocean and other geophysical fluid models.
method: Establish well-posedness, regularity and approximation theory using geometric and stochastic formulations.
Calibrate stochastic transport structures from observations and high-resolution simulations.
Develop Bayesian data assimilation using particle filters and machine-learning uncertainty quantification.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract synthesizes theoretical and methodological developments and identifies calibration data sources, but reports no quantitative benchmarks or forecast improvements.
infographic.watch_item: Practical scalability and forecasting gains in high-dimensional applications require validation beyond the evidence reported in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: From Stochastic Transport Models to High-Dimensional Bayesian Inference
